## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- **Distinguish** a law, a regulation, and a standard, and **explain** how legal duties relate to the ethics of L27. *(Understand)*
- **Identify** what **GDPR**, **HIPAA**, and **FERPA** each protect, and their core rights and de-identification ideas. *(Understand)*
- **Explain** the Puerto Rico / US jurisdictional context and the role of voluntary **standards** and governance practices. *(Understand)*
- **Apply** the right rule(s) to a data-handling scenario and say what compliance requires. *(Apply / Analyze)*

> **Where this sits:** **L27** argued what you *should* do (ethics) · this lesson covers what society made *mandatory* (the law) and walks one worked case · it **closes Unit VIII and the course** -- from "what is data science?" (L01) to governing it responsibly.

## Why This Matters

Last lesson ended on responsibility: ethics is what you should do even where no law reaches. But for a
growing share of data work, society has stopped leaving it to conscience and **written the rules down** --
with real penalties attached. Mishandle EU residents' data and the fine can reach **4% of a company's
global annual revenue**; mishandle a patient's record and HIPAA penalties (and criminal liability) follow;
mishandle a student's transcript and FERPA puts an institution's federal funding at risk.

For a data scientist this is not a reason to fear the law -- it is a reason to **know which rules touch
your data before you touch it**: what you may collect, for what purpose, how long you may keep it, what
you must let people do with their own data, and what legally counts as "de-identified". This lesson maps
that terrain, then walks one case end to end, so the rules become a **checklist you can run** rather than a
wall you hit after launch.

> **Orientation, not legal advice.** This lesson teaches what these rules require *of your data work* and
> when to bring in a lawyer. Laws change and vary by jurisdiction; for any real decision, consult counsel
> and the current official text.

## Law vs. Regulation vs. Standard

Three words that are often blurred:

- A **law / regulation** is **mandatory** -- enacted by a government, enforced with penalties. (In common
  use, a *statute* is passed by a legislature and a *regulation* is the detailed rule an agency writes to
  implement it; for our purposes both are binding.)
- A **standard** is **voluntary** -- a best-practice framework published by a standards body (ISO, NIST).
  You are not jailed for ignoring it, but customers and contracts increasingly require it, and following
  it is strong evidence of due diligence.

Recall L27: **the law is the floor, not the ceiling.** Compliance is the minimum; plenty that is legal can
still be unethical. Law tells you what you *must* do; ethics still asks what you *should*.

```{mermaid}

    Q1 -->|Yes| Q2{What kind of data,<br/>and whose?}
    Q2 -->|Health / treatment| H[HIPAA<br/>PHI, covered entities]
    Q2 -->|Student education records| F[FERPA<br/>disclosure needs consent]
    Q2 -->|EU residents' data| G[GDPR<br/>principles + data-subject rights]
    Q2 -->|Anyone, in Puerto Rico| P[US federal law applies<br/>+ PR Act 111-2005 breach notice]
```

### GDPR -- the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (in force 2018)

The most influential data law in the world; it applies **extraterritorially** -- if you process the
personal data of people in the EU, it reaches you wherever you are. It is built on a set of **principles**
for handling personal data:

- **Lawfulness, fairness, transparency** -- have a legal basis and be open about it.
- **Purpose limitation** -- collect for a specific stated purpose; do not silently reuse it for another.
- **Data minimization** -- collect only what you actually need.
- **Accuracy**, **storage limitation** (do not keep it forever), and **accountability** (you must be able
  to *show* compliance).

And it grants people **data-subject rights** over their own data: **access** (get a copy), **rectification**
(fix errors), **erasure** (the "right to be forgotten"), **portability** (take it elsewhere), and the right
to **object**. The penalties are real -- up to the greater of a large fixed sum or **4% of global annual
turnover** -- which is why GDPR reshaped industry practice worldwide.

### HIPAA -- US health-information privacy (1996)

HIPAA protects **PHI (Protected Health Information)** -- identifiable health and treatment data -- held by
**covered entities** (health providers, plans, and clearinghouses) and their business associates. Its
Privacy Rule limits how PHI may be used and shared. Crucially for a data scientist, it defines when data
counts as **de-identified** and so escapes most of the rule -- the **Safe Harbor** method requires removing
**18 specified identifiers** (names, full dates, ZIP codes beyond the first three digits, record numbers,
and so on). This is exactly L27's lesson in legal form: **stripping a name is not enough**; de-identification
is a defined, demanding standard, because combinations of attributes re-identify people.

### FERPA -- US student-education-records privacy (1974)

FERPA protects students' **education records** at institutions that receive federal funding. It gives
students (or parents, until the student is 18 or in college) the right to **access and amend** their
records, and generally **requires consent before the institution discloses** personally identifiable
information from those records to a third party (with specific exceptions, such as school officials with a
legitimate educational interest). For a university data project, FERPA is usually the first rule in the
room.

## The Puerto Rico / US Context

Puerto Rico is a **US territory**, so **US federal laws -- including HIPAA and FERPA -- apply here** just as
on the mainland. On top of the federal floor, Puerto Rico has its **own** data-protection statutes; the
most relevant is **Act No. 111 of 2005** (the citizen-information / data-bank security act), which requires
notifying people when a security breach exposes their personal information. The practical lesson:
**know your jurisdiction** -- the rules are the union of the federal laws, the local laws, and (if your
users are elsewhere) their laws too. (As always, verify the current statute and consult counsel.)

## Standards and Governance

Beyond binding law sit **voluntary standards** that organizations adopt to *demonstrate* good practice:

- **ISO/IEC 27001** -- the international standard for an information-security management system (ISMS);
  organizations get **certified** against it.
- **NIST** frameworks (US) -- the Cybersecurity Framework and the Privacy Framework, widely used reference
  models.

Following a standard is not the same as following the law, but it is how most organizations *operationalize*
the law. The governance practices you will meet on the job:

- **Privacy by design** -- build protection in from the start, not bolted on after.
- **Data minimization & purpose limitation** -- the GDPR principles, applied as daily habits. (This is the
  same instinct as L11/L15's "which features do we actually need?" -- now a legal duty.)
- A **DPIA** (Data Protection Impact Assessment) -- a structured risk review before a high-risk project.
- The **DPO** (Data Protection Officer) -- the person accountable for compliance.

## Worked Case Study: a university clinic shares athlete data

A Puerto Rico university's health clinic wants to share **student-athletes' injury and treatment data**
with an outside sports-analytics company to build a recovery-prediction model. Which rules apply, and what
must happen first? Walk it like a checklist.

1. **Identify the data and the actors.** The records are *student* records held by a *school* -- and they
   are *health/treatment* data -- and the recipient is an *outside company*. Three overlaps at once.
2. **FERPA** (education records). The data is part of the students' education records, so disclosing it to
   a third party generally needs **written consent**, unless a specific exception (e.g. a properly
   structured "school official"/vendor arrangement with control over the data) applies.
3. **HIPAA** (health data). If the clinic is a covered entity, the treatment data is **PHI**; sharing it
   requires either authorization or proper **de-identification** -- and de-identification means the
   **Safe Harbor 18 identifiers**, not just dropping names. (Whether campus health-clinic records fall
   under HIPAA or under FERPA's "treatment records" is itself a question for counsel -- exactly the kind of
   overlap you flag rather than guess.)
4. **Minimization & purpose limitation.** Share only the fields the model actually needs, for the stated
   recovery-prediction purpose only -- not "all the data, in case it is useful". A written agreement binds
   the vendor to that purpose.
5. **Breach duty (PR Act 111-2005).** If identifiable data is shared and later leaks, Puerto Rico law
   requires notifying the affected people.
6. **GDPR reach.** If any athletes are EU residents (an exchange student, say), GDPR applies to their data
   regardless of where the processing happens.

**The decision:** do not hand over the raw records. De-identify to the Safe Harbor standard (or obtain
explicit consent), share only the minimal fields under a purpose-limited agreement, document the analysis,
and have counsel review before anything moves. That is compliance -- and, not coincidentally, it is also
the ethical answer from L27.

## Your Role -- and Closing the Course

You are not the lawyer. But you are the person who knows **exactly what data flows where**, which makes you
the one who can flag a problem while it is still cheap to fix. Build compliance in early: **minimize,
document, de-identify, and ask counsel when unsure.** "I just built the model" was not a defense in L27,
and it is not one here either.

> **Course close.** You started at "what is data science?" (L01) and built outward: acquiring data at scale
> (Unit II), exploring it (Unit III), engineering and selecting features (Unit IV), visualizing and reducing
> it (Unit V), the linear algebra underneath (L18), recommending (Unit VI), and networks (Unit VII). Unit
> VIII closed the loop with the two obligations that make all of it *professional* rather than merely
> technical: **ethics** -- what you should do -- and **law** -- what you must. Carry both into every project.

## FAQ

**If data is de-identified, is it still regulated?**
Largely not -- but only if it is *truly* de-identified to the legal standard (for HIPAA, the Safe Harbor 18
identifiers or an expert determination). Naive anonymization (just dropping names) does **not** clear the
bar, because re-identification is possible (L27). Done properly, de-identification is the main lawful path
to sharing health data for analysis.

**Does GDPR apply to us in Puerto Rico?**
It can. GDPR is **extraterritorial**: if you process the personal data of people who are in the EU (offering
them goods/services or monitoring them), it applies regardless of where you or your servers are. For a
purely local PR/US audience it usually does not -- but the moment your users include EU residents, it does.

**Is following the standard the same as following the law?**
No. A standard (ISO 27001, NIST) is voluntary best practice; a law is mandatory. Following a standard helps
you comply and shows due diligence, but it does not replace the legal requirements -- and the law can demand
things no standard covers.

**Do I need to memorize statute article numbers and fine amounts?**
No. Know *which rule governs which data* and *what it requires of your work* -- and know when to call
counsel. The specifics are looked up, not memorized.

## Where to Go Deeper

- **GDPR** -- the official EU summary and full text at `gdpr.eu` / the European Commission's data-protection
  pages.
- **HIPAA** -- the US Department of Health & Human Services HIPAA Privacy Rule summary (`hhs.gov`), including
  the de-identification guidance.
- **FERPA** -- the US Department of Education Student Privacy Policy Office (`studentprivacy.ed.gov`).
- **ISO/IEC 27001** -- the ISO standard overview page; and the **NIST** Privacy Framework
  (`nist.gov/privacy-framework`).
- **Puerto Rico** -- Act No. 111 of 2005 on citizen information / data-bank security (verify the current
  consolidated text and any amendments).
